summary: NFS version 4 minor version 2 extends minor version 1. This standards-track RFC describes the additions, including Server-Side Copy, Application I/O Advise, Space Reservations, Sparse Files, Application Data Blocks and Labeled NFS.

plainLanguage.summary: NFSv4.2 adds optional operations that let clients use more server-side file-system features. A client can request copies without relaying file data, handle sparse-file holes efficiently, reserve space, send I/O hints, and work with security labels, while the protocol remains an extension of NFSv4.1.

what does read_plus do in nfsv4.2
subtitle: Adds optional copy, sparse-file, space-management, and security-label features to NFSv4.

tldr.problem: Applications need file operations such as remote copies, sparse-file handling, space reservation, and security labels without moving all file data through the client.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4.2 extends NFSv4.1 with optional operations for server-side copy, I/O hints, sparse files, space reservation, application data blocks, and labeled NFS.
tldr.outcome: Clients can ask servers to perform or optimize file operations while keeping NFSv4.1 as the base protocol. RFC 7862 is updated by RFC 8178.

today: RFC 7862 is a Proposed Standard for NFSv4.2 and is updated by RFC 8178.

sections.title: An Extension to NFSv4.1
sections.content:
NFSv4.2 is a minor version of the Network File System version 4 protocol and extends NFSv4.1. It is a superset of NFSv4.1, and the new features are optional.

The goal is to make common local file-system features available remotely. An implementation must support the required NFSv4.1 features before adding NFSv4.2 operations; the full external data representation is specified separately in RFC 7863.
sections.plainLanguage: NFSv4.2 adds optional capabilities to NFSv4.1 rather than replacing its foundation. Servers and clients can use new file operations when both sides support them.

sections.title: Copying Data on the Server
sections.content:
The COPY operation asks a server to copy file data without sending it to the client and back. It can copy within one server or between servers, and the server may complete it synchronously or report progress asynchronously.

For an asynchronous copy, the server gives the client a state identifier to poll or cancel the operation and can later report completion with a callback. CLONE provides a synchronous, atomic copy-like operation between files on the same server.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask the server to copy data directly, avoiding a trip through the client's network connection. Long copies can run asynchronously and report their results later.

sections.title: Working with Sparse Files
sections.content:
A sparse file contains holes: ranges that read as zero but do not necessarily occupy disk space. Ordinary reads may transfer those zero bytes across the network.

READ_PLUS can describe a hole instead of sending its zero-filled contents, and DEALLOCATE can punch a hole in a file. SEEK can find the next data or hole, while ALLOCATE can reserve space so future writes to a successfully reserved region do not fail for lack of space.
sections.plainLanguage: Sparse files contain empty ranges that behave as zeros. NFSv4.2 can describe those ranges without transferring every zero and can release or reserve file space explicitly.

sections.title: Hints and Application Data Blocks
sections.content:
IO_ADVISE lets a client tell the server about expected access patterns, such as sequential or random reads. A server may use the hint to change caching or prefetching, but it is not required to do so.

WRITE_SAME supports writing an application data block pattern repeatedly into a file. Other new operations report layout errors and statistics to the metadata server so it can receive information about storage-device behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can send hints about how it expects to use a file, and the server may use them to optimize its work. NFSv4.2 also adds tools for repeated data patterns and reporting storage-layout information.

sections.title: Labeled NFS and Security
sections.content:
Labeled NFS adds a sec_label file attribute so servers can store mandatory-access-control labels that clients can retrieve and use when enforcing data access. The label format is designed to accommodate different MAC systems.

NFSv4.2 also inherits NFSv4.1 security concerns and adds those associated with server-side copying and labeled NFS. The RFC discusses protecting inter-server copy authorization and security labels; deployments need the appropriate NFS security and access-control mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A security label carries access-control information with a file so a client can apply its security policy. Server-side copies and labels must be handled under the NFS security model.
